section_1.title: Geometric Intuition: The Projection
section_1.content: Define the dot product as a measure of how much one vector 'shadows' or projects onto another. Use a visual of a sun shining directly above one vector, casting a shadow of the other onto a line.
section_1.example: A hiker climbing a hill: The dot product shows how much of the hiker's movement is actually 'uphill' versus 'flat distance'.

section_2.title: The Algebraic Bridge
section_2.content: Introduce the standard formula: a · b = |a||b|cos(θ). Explain that this connects the coordinate-based calculation to the geometric behavior, forming the foundation for duality.
section_2.example: Calculating the work done by a robotic arm pulling a crate at an angle to the floor.

section_3.title: The Core of Duality: Vectors as Functions
section_3.content: Shift perspective: Instead of two vectors, view the dot product as a linear function. A fixed vector 'v' acts as a machine that takes in any vector 'x' and outputs a scalar. This is the dual space concept.
section_3.example: A motion-sensing security camera: The camera's orientation is the fixed vector; as a thief (vector x) walks past, the camera outputs a scalar value representing the 'detected intensity'.

section_4.title: Visualization: The Dual Nature
section_4.content: Show an animation where a vector rotates. As it rotates, the 'level sets' (the points where the dot product is constant) form lines or planes perpendicular to the vector.
section_4.example: Contour lines on a map: The vector points in the direction of the steepest slope, while the level lines represent the 'dual' landscape of constant elevation.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Conclude that dot products translate geometric relationships into numbers, and duality tells us that vectors aren't just arrows—they are the 'measuring devices' for the space they inhabit.
section_5.example: An artificial intelligence weighting system: Each feature (vector) is multiplied by a weight, essentially projecting the data onto a decision axis.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Center the 6x6 grid in the right half of the screen
                x = 3.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
